newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch closing debt market report.
newsitem.headline: Dutch closing debt market report.

text.p: Dutch bond dealers welcomed an "ideal" Netherlands' 1997 budget, pushing the 10-year benchmark yield almost below the key 6.00 percent threshhold.

"This is a perfect budget for the bond market. It might be a little too optimistic on some points, but even so it stands out in Europe. And that's what it all about,.. the comparison," said Hans Honig at Rabobank.

The main feature was the release of new borrowing requirement data for 1996 and 1997, revealing a scant issuing calendar for the remainder of this year and the whole of next year, underlining the scarcity of guilder bonds.

The 1996 borrowing requirement was cut to 35.1 billion guilders from over 40 billion while 1997's official requirement was estimated at 33.5 billion. However, this is before factoring in newly available state cash reserves of some 10 billion guilders which will be used to fund one-third of this amount.
"With such an empty borrowing requirement, we stand a good chance that we won't see a new 10-year bond issue before the traditional 1997 frontload in December," Honig said.
The January 2006 benchmark yielded 6.03 percent, three basis points down from Monday and at a strong 13 basis point discount to the April 2006 German bond benchmark.
Other factors were mostly priced in as most budget information had already leaked to the press in previous weeks.
Among many positive factors, such as a budget deficit of 2.2 percent of GDP, inflation stood out as a negative one.

Consumer prices are seen rising 2.5 percent in 1997, 0.25 percentage points above the European average and a full point above Germany and France. But this did not suprise dealers and analysts who said that the Central Planning Bureau had correctly anticipated the inflationary effects of stronger growth.
"They expect demands for a 2.5 percent increase in wages versus 1.5 percent this year. We think that's fair," one said.
Meanwhile, guilder bonds were not seen rising much further in the near future.
"Germany and France will show further signs of economic recovery, EMU will continue to cause some turmoil and economic growth and rate hikes in the U.S. will be a negative factor," one said.
Another said end-investors, who have been sidelined for many months, had missed the latest rally and could certainly not be tempted to buy at the current year highs.
